caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 334 of 1988 with Civil Rule No. 84 (F.M.) of 1988.
lawyer:
Rafiqur Rahman with Nurul Huq, Matiur Rahman and Serajur Rahman, Advocates  -------- For the Appellant.
 No one  -------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Muhammad Raushan Ali -------- Appellant
Vs.
Bangladesh Bar Council & Ors ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
11. Together with the oral evidence there are other evidence on record. One is the application for compromise dated 30.5.86 signed by Angur Begum and the Advocate-opposite party Mr. Roushan Ali. Another application was filed by Angur Begum on 12.7.86. She filed the application by herself and on behalf of her husband Moslemuddin stating that since there was a compromise she received the entire amount of Taka 10,000/- and she did not like to proceed with the case. Ext. 'Ga' shows that the Manager, Sonali Bank, Supreme Court Branch, Dhaka issued a certificate stating that the complainant Moslemuddin encashed Taka 10,000/- by cheque No. 295921 dated 31.5.86 issued by Mr. Roushan Ali in favour of Moslemuddin. These are more or less the oral as well as the documentary evidence in the present case. 

 21. The most important factor in this case is' the compromise effected between the parties during' the pendency of the case. For consideration of this aspect we may quote the orders dated 31.5.86, 12.6.86, 19.6.86 and 28.6.86 from the order sheet of the Tribunal which are as follows:- 

 "31.5.86 Parties present. Complainant has filed an application stating that the case is being compromised out' of Court. Hence, he does not want to proceed with the case. The complainant's wife present in Court arid she has voluntarily shown us an NC crossed cheque on Sonali Bank dated 31.5.86 in favour of complainant Mohammad Moslemuddin for Taka 10,000/- only given by the O.P. Mr. Roushan Ali, Advocate, not to be encashed on or before 10.6.86. This is a good gesture of compromise out of Court. Let the matter stand over till 12.6.1986. 

 22. From the aforesaid orders it appears that on 31.5.86 both the complainant and his wife Angur Begum as well as the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali were present and the parties had effected a compromise between them and as per term of the compromise the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali had given a crossed cheque dated 31.5.86 on Sonali Bank in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin for a sum of Tk. 10,000/- not to be encashed on or before 10.6.86. The Tribunal in the said order stated that this is a good gestures of compromise out of Court. So, it appears that with the consent as well as within the knowledge of the Tribunal the parties had effected the compromise. From Ext'. Ga' it appears that the complainant Moslemuddin encashed the aforesaid NC payee cheque-amount of Tk. 10,000/- in fulfilment of the terms of compromise. 

 23. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman submits that there is no legal bar in effecting such a compromise in a case before the Bar Council Tribunal. In a case like this the grievances of a client can be compensated generally in terms of money. It is not like a noncompoundable criminal offence. If a lawyer is found guilty of professional or other misconduct, a Tribunal may reprimand him or suspend him for some period or remove him from practice. Except the above, the Tribunal has no other power to award any other punishment. It is not a criminal Court. It is an investigative authority like an inquiry committee in c a disciplinary proceedings with the added power to award certain specific and limited punishment if it finds the Advocate to be guilty. There is no legal bar either in P.O. No. 46 of 1972 or in the relevant Rules made thereunder to effect a compromise between the parties before the Tribunal since the misconduct complained against is not a non" compoundable criminal offence. The parties, therefore, may effect a compromise in a case of this nature before the Tribunal provided it is made bonafide with the consent of the parties and the Tribunal and it is not against any law or public policy. Article 35 of P.O. 46 of 1972 provides that for the purpose of inquiry the Tribunal shall have the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of only 3 specific matters and every such inquiry shall be deemed to be a judicial d proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Penal Code and a Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for the purposes of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. These indicate that the proceeding before a Tribunal is of a civil nature and as such there appears to be no bar to effect a compromise between the parties in a proceeding before the Tribunal. 

 24. In the present case, the most unfortunate thing is that the former members of the, Tribunal could not pass a formal and final order before 12.7.86 accepting compromise and dismissing the v. petition of complaint in terms of compromise. On 28.6.86 the previous members of the Tribunal No. II passed their last order. On 19.11.86 the new members of the Tribunal took up the case for necessary order. From the order sheet it appears that the new members of the Tribunal directed to issue notices under registered post-with AID on 19.11.86, 13.12.86 and 27.1.87 upon the complainant asking him to appear. The order dated 13.12.86 shows that the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali appeared before the Tribunal and prayed for recording the. compromise. The complainant was not present and did not take any further interest in the matter, but the new Tribunal did not accept the compromise and again notice under registered post was issued upon the complainant. In spite of the issue of the above registered notices the complainant did not care to appear before the Tribunal on 12.2.87, 22.3.87, 27.4.87 and 6.6.87. Ultimately he was made to appear on 21.6.87 when he engaged a different Advocate, gave him power and filed an application stating that he was not a party to the compromise as it was not signed by him, but it was signed by his wife and the appellant-Advocate Mr. Roushan Ali. Further, he claimed refund of the remaining sum of Taka 5,000/- from the appellant. 

 25. The property in question is in the name of the complainant's wife Angur Begum. Angur Begum executed vokalatnama in favour of the appellant, but it is the husband of Angur Begum, namely, the complainant Moslemuddin who filed this complaint petition before the Bar Council. So, the complainant in fact had no cause of his own. He was defending the interest of his wife before the Tribunal. In fact, if the Tribunal wanted to be technical, it could return the petition of complaint to the complainant, asking him to submit proper petition of complaint from his wife. When the said Angur Begum herself comes and files an application for compromise stating that she received Tic. 10,000/- from the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali and that she will not proceed with the case and when the complainant Moslemuddin is also present in the proceedings, raising no objections, we find no illegality in the matter of compromise and it ought to have been accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the order dated 31.5.86 clearly shows that on that date the complainant Moslemuddin and his wife Angur Begum were both present before the Tribunal and Angur Begum received the crossed cheque dated 31.5.86 of Tk. 10,000/- from the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali and that cheque was issued in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin who himself encashed the same subsequently as per Exhibit 'Ga'. Though the complainant himself did not put his signature in the compromise petition, he was very much a party to the compromise as well as a direct beneficiary of the compromise. The compromise was acted upon. Ext'. Ga' shows that the crossed cheque issued in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin was encashed by Moslemuddin himself. By order dated 21.6.87 the Tribunal rejected the petition of compromise recording the complaint statement that he wants Tk. 5,000/- more, the balance sum. The Tribunal behaved rather strangely. Fees paid to a lawyer for professional services is not a loan. The complainant was not entitled to receive back from the appellant a single farthing. He did not file a Money suit for Tk. 15,000/- before the Tribunal. He received Tk. 10,000/- from the appellant, not as a refund of money paid, but as a compromise sum. The Tribunal failed to realise that the complainant was blowing hot and cold at the same time. He was allowed by the Tribunal to approbate and reprobate. We cannot help finding that it is the new members of the Tribunal who gave the complainant this new-found indulgence. The matter was nearly over. The new members of the Tribunal dug it up and carried it to an extreme. 

 26. The Tribunal further found that payment of Tk. 10,000/- to Moslemuddin by the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali as a matter of compromise further proved the misconduct of the appellant by admission. Such a finding cannot stand the legal test. When a compromise is effected between the parties out of Court, its terms, conditions or merit or demerit should not be questioned inasmuch as it is done by the consenting parties out of their free will without prejudice to their respective cases and the Tribunal is only to sec whether it is done bonafide or not. It is indeed unheard of that the terms of an amicable compromise reached between the parties out of Court and without prejudice to their respective cases were taken by a Tribunal as an evidence and a proof of commission of offence by one of the parties to the compromise. 

 27. In view of the above Dr. Rahman lastly submits that he does not like to argue about the malafide intention of the members of the Tribunal, but he will not be wrong if he argues that the members of the Tribunal were not at all fair in dealing with the matter of compromise in this particular case. In order to consider this point we may pose the following questions. 

 (a) What led the Members of the Tribunal to reject the compromise showing total disrespect to the former members of the Tribunal, as expressed in their order dated 31.5.86 and 12.6.86. 

 (b) What interests prompted the Members of the Tribunal to issue notices again and again upon the complainant and drag the proceeding for several months while the complainant did not care to appear before the Tribunal ignoring the prayer of Mr. Roushan Ali for disposing of the case in terms of compromise? 

 (c) Why did the Members of the Tribunal after rejecting the compromise, not compel the complainant to refund Tk. 10,000/- to Mr. Roushan Ali when the complainant repudiated the compromise and wanted to proceed with the case? Who will now be responsible for refund of Tk. 10,000/- to the appellant with interest? 

 28. From the records it is found that with the knowledge and consent of the Tribunal (while the former members were sitting) the compromise was effected and the Tribunal encouraged such compromise, but owing to some technical difficulty it could not record the final order. In spite of the fact that the complainant was a consenting party as well as a direct beneficiary to the compromise, the Members of the Tribunal illegally rejected the compromise for no reason or for reasons best known to them. Again, the order-sheets of the case show that the Members of Tribunal were waiting and waiting for the complainant and they were in fact bent upon making him appear before the Tribunal while the complainant himself had lost all interest in the case. Further, when the Members were successful in bringing the complainant before the Tribunal, how could they allow him to repudiate the compromise and proceed with the case on the face of Ext "Ga' which shows that the complainant personally received Tk. 10,000/- through cheque from the appellant in fulfilment of the terms of compromise. All these unmistakably lend support to the last contention of Dr. Rahman that the Members of the Tribunal had not fairly dealt with the present case, particularly the compromise chapter. In our view, after effecting the compromise there was nothing for adjudication in the present case and the Members in fact made a mountain out of a molehill for no reasons whatsoever.
